title: Domain IV: Procurement Business Principles - Procurement Business Principles - Roles & Responsibilities
subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: Under the Law of Agency, what defines the relationship between a Principal and an Agent?
options: The Agent is a vendor selling goods to the Principal.
The Agent is authorized to act on behalf of and bind the Principal in transactions with third parties.
The Principal relies on the Agent for funding.
The Agent is entirely immune from any legal action.
questions.explain: In an agency relationship, the Principal (the government entity) grants authority to an Agent (the procurement officer) to act and form contracts on its behalf.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: A procurement officer's 'Express Authority' is derived from:
options: The officer's personal experience and tenure.
The vendor's belief that the officer can sign the contract.
Written or spoken delegations such as statutes, ordinances, or a procurement manual.
The actions commonly expected of a buyer in the private sector.
questions.explain: Express authority is explicitly granted to the agent in clear, direct terms, typically through laws, policies, or formal job descriptions.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: What type of authority gives a procurement professional the right to perform incidental actions necessary to carry out their express duties?
questions.explain: Implied authority is not explicitly stated but is deemed reasonably necessary for the agent to effectively perform the duties for which they have express authority.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: An IT manager (who is not a procurement officer) tells a software vendor to upgrade 100 licenses, and the vendor complies, believing the manager had the power to do so. In this scenario, what kind of authority did the vendor rely on?
questions.explain: Apparent authority occurs when a third party reasonably believes someone has authority based on the principal's conduct, even though the person lacks actual express authority. Note: Public entities are often protected against claims of apparent authority.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: When a public employee makes a purchase outside the bounds of their legal authority, the act is known in law as:
questions.explain: 'Ultra vires' translates to 'beyond the powers.' An ultra vires act is one taken by an agent that goes beyond their legal authority, rendering the contract potentially void.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: In public procurement, which principle is intended to prevent fraud and errors by ensuring that no single individual controls all phases of a transaction?
questions.explain: Segregation of duties separates crucial functions—such as ordering, receiving, and authorizing payment—so that no one person has total control over a transaction.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: Which of the following scenarios best demonstrates proper segregation of duties?
options: The buyer generates the PO, receives the goods in the system, and approves the invoice.
The end-user requests the item, the buyer issues the PO, and accounts payable cuts the check.
The warehouse manager negotiates the contract, signs the PO, and accepts delivery.
The vendor creates the requirement, quotes the price, and receives payment directly.
questions.explain: In option B, the request, authorization/procurement, and payment are handled by separate individuals/departments, creating necessary checks and balances.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: A procurement official acts as an agent and has a 'Fiduciary Duty' to the principal. Fiduciary duty primarily requires the agent to:
options: Obtain the highest possible profit for vendors.
Act with the highest standard of care, loyalty, and honesty in the best interest of the principal.
Spend exactly the budget allocated, no more and no less.
questions.explain: Fiduciary duty is a legal obligation of one party to act in the best interest of another. The buyer must act loyally and ethically for the public entity.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: An unauthorized commitment (ultra vires act) is made by a department head. Later, the Chief Procurement Officer formally accepts and approves the transaction. This legal action is called:
questions.explain: Ratification is the retroactive approval of an unauthorized act. Once ratified by an individual with proper authority, the contract becomes legally binding on the entity.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: What happens when a private vendor relies on the 'apparent authority' of a public official who did not have actual authority?
options: The contract is always fully enforceable against the public entity.
The public entity is usually not bound, and the vendor may suffer a loss because apparent authority generally does not apply to governments.
The government is required to pay double damages to the vendor.
questions.explain: Unlike the private sector, courts generally hold that anyone dealing with a government entity must ascertain the limits of the agent's authority. Apparent authority rarely binds a government.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: A buyer purchases stock in a company, and the next week advocates for awarding a sole-source contract to that same company. What fiduciary concept has the buyer violated?
questions.explain: The Duty of Loyalty requires the agent to avoid conflicts of interest and not benefit personally from transactions made on behalf of the principal.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: In a decentralized procurement model, end-users are given Procurement Cards (P-Cards) to buy small-dollar items. This process represents:
options: A formal delegation of purchasing authority.
questions.explain: Distributing P-Cards with defined spending limits and rules is a planned, legal delegation of micro-purchasing authority to end-users to increase efficiency.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: If a government employee commits an unauthorized act knowingly and with malicious intent, and the entity refuses to ratify it, who can the vendor legally hold liable?
questions.explain: If an agent acts entirely outside their authority without agency ratification, the agent can be held personally liable by the third party for the unauthorized commitment.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: Which individual typically holds the highest level of delegated administrative procurement authority within a public entity?
options: Chief Procurement Officer (CPO) or Purchasing Director
questions.explain: The Chief Procurement Officer (CPO) usually receives the highest delegation of purchasing authority directly from the governing board or executive to manage agency-wide procurement.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: A mayor verbally instructs a buyer to award a contract to a friend. The city charter dictates awards over a certain amount require City Council approval. If the buyer complies, this act is:
options: Valid through the mayor's inherent authority.
Invalid and an ultra vires act.
A prime example of ethical delegation.
questions.explain: Since the city charter expressly requires Council approval, bypassing it violates statutory bounds, making the award an unauthorized (ultra vires) act, regardless of the mayor's instruction.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: In standard roles and responsibilities, who is primarily responsible for drafting the technical scope of work (SOW)?
questions.explain: The requesting department holds the technical expertise to define what they need, while procurement ensures the SOW is not restrictive and adheres to legal standards.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: Which principle limits a vendor's ability to sue a state government for breach of contract, requiring the state to consent to be sued?
questions.explain: Sovereign immunity is the legal doctrine whereby a sovereign or state cannot commit a legal wrong and is immune from civil suit or criminal prosecution unless it waives that immunity.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: Under the Law of Agency, what happens to the agent's authority if the principal (e.g., the government entity) ceases to exist?
options: The agent must find a new principal within 30 days.
questions.explain: Agency law states that the agent's power strictly derives from the principal. If the principal ceases to exist (or revokes the authority), the agent's authority is immediately terminated.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: An agency's policy states buyers can sign contracts up to $50,000. A buyer signs a contract for $75,000. What defense protects the government from fulfilling the $75,000 contract?
options: The buyer exceeded their actual authority, and apparent authority typically does not bind governments.
The contract was signed in black ink.
questions.explain: Because the buyer exceeded the $50,000 limit, they lacked actual authority. Vendors are legally obligated to know the bounds of a public agent's authority, so the government isn't bound.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: When establishing an evaluation committee, why should the procurement officer limit the participation of the ultimate decision-maker (e.g., the Agency Director)?
options: Directors do not have time to read proposals.
To maintain segregation of duties between evaluation and the final award authorization.
To force vendors to present to lower-level staff.
questions.explain: Having the final award authority participate in the evaluation committee removes the checks and balances designed to prevent undue influence and ensure an objective process.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: What does 'Estoppel' mean in the context of agency and authority?
options: The principal is prevented from denying the existence of an agency relationship if their actions previously suggested it existed to a third party.
Stopping a vendor from submitting bids.
A legal mandate to issue RFPs.
questions.explain: Promissory estoppel prevents a principal from going back on a representation if a third party reasonably relied on that representation to their detriment. (Though highly restricted against public entities).
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: In local government, the highest level of procurement authority typically resides with the:
options: Governing Body (e.g., City Council or Board of Commissioners)
questions.explain: The ultimate statutory and financial authority for a local government resides with the elected governing body, which then delegates operating authority to the executive and CPO.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: A procurement agent makes a mathematical error on a purchase order that favors the vendor. Does the vendor have the right to enforce the erroneous higher price?
options: No, unilateral mathematical errors (clerical errors) that are obvious typically do not bind the agency.
No, because vendors are not allowed to make profit on public contracts.
questions.explain: In contract law, obvious unilateral mistakes, particularly clerical or mathematical errors that the other party should reasonably recognize, do not create a binding obligation at the erroneous price.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: To prevent unauthorized commitments (after-the-fact purchases), what is the most effective proactive control an agency can implement?
options: Require a valid Purchase Order number to be issued before goods or services can be ordered.
questions.explain: A strict 'No PO, No Pay' policy ensures funds are encumbered and authorized before a transaction takes place, eliminating unauthorized after-the-fact commitments.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: When a central procurement office establishes agency-wide term contracts for common commodities, how does it handle actual ordering authority?
options: Procurement makes every single order and stores the goods.
It delegates the ordering authority to end-users to place releases against the master contract as needed.
It forces vendors to guess the quantity and ship randomly.
It requires the City Council to approve each individual order.
questions.explain: Establishing master agreements is a central procurement role; delegating the actual call-off or release orders to end-users balances central control with decentralized operational efficiency.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles
